_doc: Single source for SD-47's technology choices; see SD-08/stack.json for the format. `how` is spoken, so it carries no code; keep summary cells under 36 characters.

stack.heading: Inventory DB: PostgreSQL, one conditional statement
stack.title: One statement is the check and the change
stack.pick: PostgreSQL 16, primary and synchronous standby, read committed
stack.why: Selling a seat once is a conditional update on a row, in a transaction with the hold and the outbox. Row locks and constraints are the tools that make it true.
stack.how: Each seat of each event is a row with a state. A claim is one update statement that names the state it expects: set held where the seat is free. A second fan's identical statement matches no row and learns the seat is taken. The hold row and the outbox row commit in the same transaction. Read committed is enough because the check and the change are the same statement.
stack.detail: The database is partitioned by event, so a hot on-sale loads one partition.
rejected: Read the seat, then update it
Two fans both read free and both write. The conditional update closes the gap in one statement.
Redis for the hold
A key can expire or vanish while the database still says held. The hold belongs in the same transaction as the seat.
A distributed lock per seat
One more system, and a lock without a token has the stale-holder failure.
summary: Check and change are one statement
stack.course: theory/03 (partitioning and storage) and theory/07 (correctness under failure)
drill: Ten thousand fans click the same seat in the same second. What does the database do?
Ten thousand identical conditional updates queue on one row; the first matches, the other 9,999 match nothing and return taken. The trap is a read-then-write in the application.
one conditional update; the losers match nothing

stack.heading: Waiting room: Redis with Lua
stack.title: A line held in memory, advanced by a pointer
stack.pick: Redis, a sorted set for the lobby, a pointer, Lua scripts for the atomic steps
stack.why: A million fans arriving at once cannot all reach the shop. The line is a data structure that must be fast and atomic.
stack.how: A fan joins the lobby and receives a position. An admission pointer advances at the rate the controller sets. A Lua script moves a batch from the lobby into the admitted set and mints their tokens in one atomic step, so no fan is admitted twice. Polling for position is served from a cached snapshot, not from Redis.
stack.detail: Persistence to disk is on, and the line can be rebuilt from the join log if the node is lost.
rejected: The relational database as the queue
A million inserts in a minute onto the inventory primary: the line would take the booking path down with it.
Kafka as the queue
Good for ordering, awkward for a position the fan can poll and a pointer that advances.
A third-party waiting room product
A real option; we show the design, and buy if the team cannot run it.
drill: The Redis node holding the line fails. What happens to the million fans waiting?

A replica is promoted and the line is rebuilt from the replicated state and the join log; positions may shift slightly but nobody is admitted twice, because admission is a single script. The trap is losing the line.
a replica; rebuild from the log; admission is atomic

stack.heading: Admission: a dial and a signed token
stack.title: A controller that turns one dial, and a token the gateway checks locally
stack.pick: A Go control loop, a signed token, a gateway that verifies without a database call
stack.why: The shop can serve only so many shoppers. The dial sets how many enter per second, and a signed pass proves they were let in.
stack.how: The admission controller watches the shop's load and turns the rate dial down or up. A fan reaching the pointer gets a short-lived signed token, a JWT valid for ten minutes. Every shop call carries it. The gateway verifies the signature and expiry locally, so the check costs no database call.
stack.detail: A bot farm can hold many tokens; per-fan limits sit behind the gateway.
rejected: Rate limiting at the gateway only
It rejects fans instead of queueing them: a fair line becomes a race of retries.
A session lookup per request
The session store becomes the bottleneck of the shop.

stack.heading: Seat events: Kafka with the outbox
stack.title: Every change to a seat is an event that others can consume
stack.pick: Outbox in the inventory transaction, Kafka partitioned by event
stack.why: The seat map, notifications and any later consumer need to know what changed. The event must exist if and only if the claim committed.
stack.how: Each claim, release and sale writes an outbox row in the same transaction as the seat change. A relay publishes the rows to Kafka in commit order, partitioned by event, at least once. The seat-map builder, notifications and a future waitlist are separate consumer groups, each deduplicating.
stack.detail: A waitlist, for example, is just a new consumer of this log.
rejected: Publishing after the commit
A crash between the two loses a seat change for ever.
Consumers reading the database
Every consumer adds load to the inventory primary during the sale.
summary: A waitlist is a new consumer
drill: Product wants a waitlist added mid-sale. What changes in the booking path?
Nothing. The waitlist is a new consumer group reading the seat events, and it acts on a released seat. The trap is rewriting booking.
a new consumer of the log; booking is untouched

stack.heading: CDN: the queue state and the layout
stack.title: The edge absorbs what is the same for everyone
stack.pick: A CDN with a WAF, one-second lifetimes, request collapsing
stack.why: Ten thousand shoppers asking for the same seat map should cost one origin request, not ten thousand.
stack.how: The CDN caches the immutable venue layout for a long time and the queue state for a second. When many requests for an expired object reach one point of presence, request collapsing sends one request to the origin. The WAF rejects obvious bot traffic and scripted floods before they reach the waiting room.
stack.detail: Per-fan data, like a position, is not cached at the edge; it goes through a short cached snapshot at the origin.
rejected: Serving everything from the origin
The origin would carry the whole stampede.
A long edge lifetime for seat state
Fans would see seats as free that are gone, and click into failures.

stack.heading: Seat map: layout and a versioned bitmap
stack.title: An immutable layout and a bitmap built from the event log
stack.pick: A Go service, an immutable layout object, a bitmap snapshot per event version in Redis
stack.why: Ten thousand shoppers want to see which seats are free. That must not touch the inventory primary.
stack.how: The venue layout is immutable and cached for ever. A builder consumes the seat events and writes a compact bitmap of seat states, about six kilobytes per event, to the snapshot cache under a version number. The seat-map service serves the layout plus the latest bitmap, and the client shows a fresh-as-of time.
stack.detail: A stale map can show a taken seat as free; the claim is what decides, so staleness costs a retry, not an oversell.
rejected: Querying the seat table per shopper
Ten thousand readers on the primary during the sale.
Pushing every seat change to every browser
A fan-out of every claim to ten thousand screens.
drill: The map says a seat is free and the fan clicks it, but it is gone. Is that an oversell?
No. The claim, one conditional update, decides, and answers taken; the map is a hint. The client refetches. The trap is treating the map as the truth.
the claim decides; the map is only a hint

stack.heading: Order service and the hold expirer
stack.title: A checkout saga, and a sweeper that frees what nobody paid for
stack.pick: Go order service, an idempotent payment call, a hold expirer, a reconciler
stack.why: A hold must end, whether the fan pays, abandons or the payment goes quiet. Both outcomes must be safe.
stack.how: The order service runs a saga: freeze the hold so it cannot expire mid-payment, call the payment provider with an idempotency key, then confirm the sale or release. The hold expirer sweeps holds past their time and releases them; the claim itself also expires an old hold when it finds one. A reconciler asks the provider about payments that went silent.
stack.detail: Two paths each cover the other's gap: the sweeper catches what no claim touches, and the claim catches what the sweeper has not reached.
rejected: A TTL on a Redis key as the hold
The key and the database can disagree. The hold belongs with the seat.
Releasing the hold the moment it expires
If the payment succeeded in that instant, we have taken money for a seat we resold.
drill: The hold expires, then the payment succeeds. Who gets the seat?
The fan who paid, because the hold was frozen before the call. A reconciler resolves a silent payment by asking the provider, and only then releases. The trap is releasing at expiry.
freeze before the call; reconcile silence

1: Read the seat, then update it
two fans both see free; one statement is the check and the change.
2: Holding seats in Redis with a TTL
the key and the database can disagree; two paths cover each other's gap.
3: Releasing the hold at the moment it expires
the payment may have succeeded in that instant; freeze before the call and reconcile silence.
4: Autoscaling the shop to a million at the door
scale lags the spike; a line in front and a dial behind it.
5: bots with faster connections win; a lottery for everyone present, then first-come.
6: Querying the seat table per shopper
ten thousand readers on the primary; an immutable layout and a versioned bitmap.
7: Rewriting booking to add a waitlist
a waitlist is a new consumer of the seat events, not a redesign.
8: the servers can be fine while seats sell twice; measure the promise, not the machine.
